title: slacheck: achievable SLOs for distributed applications
tagline: Given a service topology and per-service SLOs, slacheck computes the SLO the whole application can actually promise and names the sub-objective that breaks it.
problem: Teams promise an end-to-end SLA (say 99.9%) without checking it against what their dependencies deliver. The gap surfaces in production as a breached SLA, a weak dependency, or an autoscaling rule that reacts too late.
approach: The topology is a typed DAG (required vs redundant calls). Ascending aggregation composes per-service latency, error budget and cost into the achievable envelope, minus a cloud-tier safety margin. Descending decomposition splits the target into per-service thresholds weighted by structural centrality, and autoscaling triggers are checked against the operational bound that keeps the SLO.

demo.caption: pip install, then the 113-scenario evaluation (v1 67/113 vs v2 113/113), one reconfiguration fault v1 misses and v2 catches, and a 7-service shop checked against 99.9%.

limits: The 113 scenarios are a constructed dataset with injected faults: they show the mechanism, not the false-alarm rate on a real fleet.
v1 has no reconfiguration model, so its 0/43 on that class is by construction.
Live mode needs Datadog API/app keys; the showcase runs offline on fixtures.
Per-service cost is not exposed by Datadog; it comes from a YAML override or a k8s resource estimate.
